messages.subject: Single visit, multiple time intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working with some unique data, and I have not found a post in this group about how to deal with it. I am using Breeding Bird Atlas data, where each site was only visited once (ever), and for each visit, bird observations were dividing into five 75-s time intervals. Here is a short version of what the data looks like:

Site     Species       T1  T2  T3  T4  T5  Time  Date
1          NOBO         1    1    0    0    1     7:58   6-2
2          NOBO         0    0    1    0    0     7:02   6-8
2          NOBO         1    0    1    1    0     7:02   6-8
3          NOBO         0    0    0    0    1     8:35   6-9

As you can see, the challenge I'm encountering is how to deal with sites that had multiple birds detected. For sites with multiple birds, the birds often vary with regards to which time interval they were detected during. In total, there were 187 unique sites visited, but a total of 233 NOBOs recorded. I am ultimately interested in the site covs that influence occupancy, but I need to account for the observation covs. I have been creating models using the occu function, and believe that I could naively ignore any variables related to detection, in which case I could just use one of the birds per site (since the site covs would be the same). Alternatively, I have tried accounting for imperfect detection by considering each observation a "site" (i.e. 233 sites, one for each bird with site/obs covs duplicated for sites with multiple birds), but this does not seem to be a proper way to do so. The results change quite a bit depending on whether I use one bird per site (187 rows) or all birds, each considered as belonging to their own site (233 rows).

Thank you for your help, and any advice that can be provided on how I should work with this data would be much appreciated!

Best,
Connor

messages.body_plain:
Hi. I’m still analysing my point count bird data. According to MacKenzie et al. (2002): “We advise caution if an estimate of occupancy very close to 1 is obtained when detection probabilities are low (<0.15)”. I want to check this but I’m a bit unsure how to do it. I tried just simply calling one of the models to see what output I get. Here’s an example of my code:

#Read data

test_occu <- read.csv("C:/Users/PC/Documents/Examensarbete/Data/HOM_treesparrow2019.csv", dec=".", sep=";")

y <- test_occu[,2:3] #The frequencies for 1st survey and 2nd survey

siteCovs <- test_occu[,4:11] #The habitat data (occupancy cov)

obsCovs <- list(Day=test_occu[,c("Day1", "Day2")],

                Observer=test_occu[,c("Observer1", "Observer2")],

                Wind=test_occu[,c("Wind1", "Wind2")],

                Cloud=test_occu[,c("Cloud1", "Cloud2")]) #The weather, etc. (detection cov)

#Create unmaked frame

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y, siteCovs=siteCovs, obsCovs=obsCovs)

#Create models (examples)

dm1 <- occu(~ 1 ~ 1, umf) #Null model

dm3 <- occu(~ Cloud ~ 1, umf)

dm5 <- occu(~ Wind + Cloud ~ 1, umf)

dm3

#Running dm3 gives output:

Call:

occu(formula = ~Cloud ~ 1, data = umf)

Occupancy:

 Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)

   -0.153 0.198 -0.771   0.441

Detection:

            Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)

(Intercept)    0.203 0.335 0.605   0.545

Cloud          0.197 0.125 1.573   0.116

AIC: 418.5046

Can someone please help me interpret this? I’m guessing that the Intercept on detection is the null model, which is compared to the cloud covariate. So does it mean that the detection probability for the species, when using cloud as a covariate, is 0.197? That would mean that I’m just above the recommended 0.15 limit and can proceed with the analysis (model selection and stuff like that).

Or should I use some other function to check the detectability and occupancy estimates? What is the difference between doig this and a backtransformation?

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Check if detection estimate is >0.15
messages.body_plain:
You need to describe the values that Cloud can take.  If the values are just 0 and 1 (meaning maybe "not cloudy" and "cloudy", respectively?), then for "not cloudy" the probability of detection for a single visit is

    1-1/(1+exp(0.203)) = 0.5505764

and for "cloudy" the probability of detection for a single visit is

    1-1/(1+exp(0.203+0.197)) = 0.4618244

Using that standard you quote those probabilities are considerably higher than 0.15.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
OK.  Maybe you've already convinced yourself that a linear function of cloud categories (treated as numbers) is a reasonable assumption for the logits of the detection probabilities.  If you have lots of data, I would be inclined to treat the 5 values as a categorical variables (or cloud as a "factor" in R-speak) at least initially.  But that's another issue you should consider.

Here's a brute force approach to get the detection probabilities for cloud cover values of 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4:

> 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.203 + c(0:4)*0.197))
> # 0.5505764 0.5986877 0.6449697 0.6886896 0.7292854

For more complex models it's probably less user-error prone (at least for me) to use the linearComb and backTransform functions in unmarked to get the same results.

Jim

> For models with a single observational covariate rather than selecting just one predicted detection probability, I would say you want to look at all of them (with "all of them" meaning across the complete range of the values of the observational covariate).  Including confidence bands would also be warranted:  "A statistic is at best of unknown value without a measure of precision."  Here's a brute force example using data included with unmarked:
>
> > # Get data
> >   library(unmarked)
> >   pcru <- csvToUMF(system.file("csv","frog2001pcru.csv", package="unmarked"),
> >     long = TRUE, type = "unmarkedFrameOccu")
> >
> > # Run occu
> >   fm <- occu(~Temperature ~ 1, pcru, control=list(reltol=1e-12))
> >
> > # Make predictions over the range of observed temperatures
> >   tempMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   tempMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> >   temp <- tempMin + (tempMax-tempMin)*c(0:100)/100
> >   prob <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp))
> >
> > # Plot estimated detection curve
> >   plot(temp, prob, type="l", xlab="Temperature (degrees C)",
> >     ylab="Detection probability", cex.lab=1.5, font.lab=2, las=1,
> >     ylim=c(0,1), lwd=3)
> >
> > # Add in approximate 95% confidence band
> >   v <- vcov(fm)
> >   se <- (v[2,2] + temp^2 * v[3,3] + 2*temp*v[2,3])^0.5
> >   lines(temp,  1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp + 1.96*se)), lty=3)
> >   lines(temp,  1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2]+fm@opt$par[3]*temp - 1.96*se)), lty=3)
> >
> >
> >
> > When there are two observational covariates one could construct a contour plot:
> >
> > > # Get data
> > >   library(unmarked)
> > >   pcru <- csvToUMF(system.file("csv","frog2001pcru.csv", package="unmarked"),
> > >     long = TRUE, type = "unmarkedFrameOccu")
> > >
> > > # Run occu
> > >   fm2 <- occu(~ MinAfterSunset + Temperature ~ 1, pcru)
> > >
> > > # Construct contour plot on a 101 x 101 array over the observed
> > > # range of observational covariates.
> > >   masMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$MinAfterSunset, na.rm=TRUE)
> > >   masMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$MinAfterSunset, na.rm=TRUE)
> > >   tempMin <- min(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> > >   tempMax <- max(pcru@obsCovs$Temperature, na.rm=TRUE)
> > >   prob <- matrix(rep(NA,101^2), nrow=101)
> > >   mas <- masMin + (masMax-masMin)*c(0:100)/100
> > >   temp <- tempMin + (tempMax-tempMin)*c(0:100)/100
> > >   for (i in 1:101) {
> > >   for (j in 1:101) {
> > >       prob[i,j] = 1 - 1/(1+exp(sum(fm2@opt$par[2:4]*c(1, mas[i], temp[j]))))
> > >   }}
> > >   contour(mas, temp, prob, xlab="Time after sunset (min)",

> > >
> > >

Which model I should choose: 1) the model with the smallest AIC or 2) the model with significant site covariates?
Thank you very much for any comments.

Your detection output is

> Detection:
>
>             Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)

> (Intercept)    0.203 0.335 0.605   0.545
>
> Cloud          0.197 0.125 1.573   0.116

So the term coefficients=c(1,3) in backTransform(linearComb(dm3, coefficients=c(1,3), type="det")) means that to calculate the logit of the detection probability the following calculations are performed:

> logit = 1*Intercept + 3*Cloud = 1*0.203 + 3*0.197 = 0.794
>
>
Then the logit is converted to a probability:

      detection probability = 1 - 1/(1+exp(logit)) = 1- 1/(1+exp(0.794)) =  0.6886896

Jim

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Which one is more important: AIC or p value in determining the best fittest single season/species occupancy modeling?
messages.body_plain:
I have my standard statistician answer:  It depends.

It depends on more than AIC and a p-value.  Or at least it should.  If it only depended on something calculated from the data that has absolutely no subject knowledge needed, then why would we statisticians need you?

AIC is a relative rather than absolute measure of model quality.  You need to determine if the best model is good enough and not just the best one can do.  That requires subject matter knowledge (and expertise).  Maybe the 2nd best model (irrespective of significant covariates) is a lot cheaper to use or more politically acceptable to use and gives pretty much the same predictions.  I don't know.

The point is that using AIC (and other purely statistical measures) provides reasonable approaches to select models but that isn't the end of it.

OK.  End of sermon.

Jim

Aye,

For each species you should have a matrix in R with M rows (number of sites) and J columns (number of observations at each site), with each entry a 0 if that species was not detected and 1 if it was.
Then,  to make the input "y" you combine those matrices together in R into a list.

messages.subject: problems with predict() on generated variables from poly(), splines::bs(), etc.
messages.subject_clean: problems with predict() on generated variables from poly(), splines::bs(), etc.
messages.body_plain:
Hello-

I was recently working with a student who ran into problems when making predictions from pcount() using orthogonal polynomials via poly() compared to raw polynomials (fit either with I() or poly(..., raw = TRUE) ).  I poked around a bit and found that the predict methods don't appear to be working correctly for "generated" variables like those from poly(), splines::bs(), scale(), etc.  I didn't see any previous discussion about this so thought I would bring it up here.

Here's a little example to show very different predictions from a quadratic relationship fit with poly() vs I(variable^2):

library(unmarked)

data(mallard)
mallardUMF <- unmarkedFramePCount(mallard.y, siteCovs = mallard.site,
                                  obsCovs = mallard.obs)
fm.mallard1 <- pcount(~ 1 ~ elev + I(elev^2) + offset(length), mallardUMF, K = 30)
fm.mallard2 <- pcount(~ 1 ~ poly(elev, degree = 2) + offset(length), mallardUMF, K = 30)

# Take first 5 values of original data for prediction
dat = data.frame(length = mallard.site$length[1:5],
                 elev = mallard.site$elev[1:5],
                 othervar = 1:5)

# Predictions from 2 models should be same/very similar
predict(fm.mallard1, type = "state", newdata = dat)
#>    Predicted         SE      lower     upper
#> 1 1.01396362 0.14753356 0.76237912 1.3485708
#> 2 0.48184096 0.06512837 0.36970087 0.6279961
#> 3 0.08689944 0.02133615 0.05370616 0.1406080
#> 4 0.17282331 0.04419640 0.10469431 0.2852867
#> 5 0.12698742 0.01577647 0.09954293 0.1619985

predict(fm.mallard2, type = "state", newdata = dat)
#>      Predicted           SE        lower        upper
#> 1 4.994202e+02 6.322692e+02 4.176759e+01 5.971628e+03
#> 2 8.780117e+01 1.235498e+02 5.568366e+00 1.384436e+03
#> 3 1.115903e-05 2.186476e-05 2.397735e-07 5.193400e-04
#> 4 9.999348e-06 4.019014e-05 3.791035e-09 2.637458e-02
#> 5 3.372450e+00 1.019707e+01 8.999533e-03 1.263779e+03

It turns out this disparity is because the new data for predictions has a new transformation applied to it to make orthogonal variables instead of using the transformation based on the original data.  You can see this by comparing the a model.frame using the new dataset of the first 5 original values to the original transformation of the original data.

model.frame( paste0("~", fm.mallard2@formula[3]), data = dat) # new data, new transformation
#>   poly(elev, degree = 2).1 poly(elev, degree = 2).2 offset(length)
#> 1              -0.42107325               0.50870575          0.801
#> 2              -0.37760519               0.08895565          0.115
#> 3               0.50026073              -0.37353885         -0.479
#> 4               0.58814181               0.42116410          0.315
#> 5              -0.28972410              -0.64528666         -1.102

poly(mallard.site$elev, degree = 2)[1:5, ] # original data, original transformation
#>                 1           2
#> [1,] -0.076030699  0.06829479
#> [2,] -0.073048986  0.05876529
#> [3,] -0.012831347 -0.06541581
#> [4,] -0.006803101 -0.07068313
#> [5,] -0.067020740  0.04047351

Predict functions like predict.lm appear to automagically deal with orthogonal polynomials fit with poly() by keeping information on the original transformation.  This is done with the helper function makepredictcall() and the predvars argument in the terms.object function to keep the information for model.frame() to use.

There may be sophisticated ways to deal with this.  One (simplish?) approach would be to change how the model matrix is calculated in the predict functions for data.frames to carry the original transformation along with terms().  This complicates the offset calculation, though.  Something like:

formula <- fm.mallard2@formula
stateformula <- as.formula(paste0("~", formula[3]))

# Possible fix to add predvars from original data
     # for use in model matrix with terms()
terms <- terms( model.frame(stateformula, data = fm.mallard2@data@siteCovs) )

# Now the newdata data transformation matches original
( Xmat <- model.matrix(terms, data = dat) ) # new data, original transformation
#>   (Intercept) poly(elev, degree = 2)1 poly(elev, degree = 2)2
#> 1           1            -0.076030699              0.06829479
#> 2           1            -0.073048986              0.05876529
#> 3           1            -0.012831347             -0.06541581
#> 4           1            -0.006803101             -0.07068313
#> 5           1            -0.067020740              0.04047351
#> attr(,"assign")
#> [1] 0 1 1
poly(mallard.site$elev, degree = 2)[1:5, ] # original data, transformation
#>                 1           2
#> [1,] -0.076030699  0.06829479
#> [2,] -0.073048986  0.05876529
#> [3,] -0.012831347 -0.06541581
#> [4,] -0.006803101 -0.07068313
#> [5,] -0.067020740  0.04047351

# Getting offset takes an extra step
offset <- model.offset( model.frame(terms, data = dat) )

# Predictions now same to 3ish decimal places
exp( linearComb(fm.mallard2, Xmat, type = "state", offset = offset)@estimate )
#> [1] 1.01345736 0.48168078 0.08700687 0.17303138 0.12698479

predict(fm.mallard1, type = "state", newdata = dat)$Predicted
#> [1] 1.01396362 0.48184096 0.08689944 0.17282331 0.12698742

I found similar issues when I used splines::bs() and scale() directly in pcount(), which is what made me realize this may be bigger than poly().

Regards,
Ariel

Dear Atharva,

your question just makes me think that there is that alternative design for an occupancy study known as "time-to-detection" (ttd). This is a continuous-time observation protocol, where you note the time (in minutes, seconds) between the start of a survey and the moment when you detect the first individual of each species (see papers by Garrard et al., Austral Ecology, 2008, Bornand et al., MEE, 2014 among others). We also have a section on ttd designs in the AHM1 book, and Ken Kellner has recently included it into unmarked (for single species only).

The greatest thing about this design is perhaps that you can estimate occupancy and detection separately from just a single visit. Hence, in your case this would mean that you could half your survey effort or double the number of sites surveyed.

You should look into this design perhaps. It is much less well-known than the standard designs and hardly ever used, although it's been 12 years now since Garrard et al first described it. I am puzzled by the rarity of its use, since it offers such obvious logistical benefits, as one visit is already enough.

If you wanted to do multispecies analyses with data collected under this design, then you could not (currently) do this in unmarked (nor in PRESENCE or MARK, as far as I know, though I may be wrong). However, it would be trivial to fit such a community occupancy model in BUGS software (or anything else if you have a very good friend who is a statistician).

Best regards  --- Marc

Two general comments:

(1) When sampling a large population, it is the total number of samples that typically drives everything as opposed to the percent of the area being sampled.

(2) One needs to know how good the precision needs to be to judge the adequacy of the sampling.  That is a subject matter rather than a statistical issue.  Sample size and percent of area sampled cannot tell you that.

Hi Erik,

The issue is with your fitstats function. The y data, fitted data, and residuals are different in occuMulti from other unmarked functions because you have separate encounter histories for each species. These are generally stored as lists of matrices (one per species), but to calculate stats you generally want a single matrix of residual values, fitted values, etc.

One approach is to take the lists of matrices and row-bind them into a single matrix:

fitstats <- function(fit) {

  resids <- do.call(rbind, residuals(fit))
  observed <- do.call(rbind, fit@data@ylist)
  expected <- do.call(rbind, fitted(fit))

  sse <- sum(resids^2)
  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)
  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2)
  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)
  return(out)
}

This function works in parboot and should also work in mb.gof.test. However I haven't though much about the validity of combining residuals across multiple species like this.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mary,

you should initialize R’s search for the maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs) close to what you think the solutions are AND you must provide exactly one starting value per parameter, on the link scale at which computations are done.

So, in a constant model (e.g., occu(~1~1, data = UFO1)), let’s assume that your guess is that occupancy could be about 0.8 and detection about 0.3. Then, you could do this:

inits <- qlogis(c(0.8, 0.3))

fm <- occu(~1~1, data = UFO1, starts = inits)

A little confusingly, the order of parameters is different in the model formula (where detection comes before occupancy) and in the output from the model fitting function, where occupancy comes first, as you can also see by doing this:

coef(fm). In the list of starting values, you must choose the latter order, i.e., occupancy parameters come first. In any unmarked fitting function you can check the right order of the parameters for input as starting values by doing coef(fm).

In your second model, assuming that veg_group2 is either a two-level factor or a continuous explanatory variable for occupancy, you seem to provide 4 inits where 3 are required. Could that be the problem ? And if that is not the problem, then you may have to tune your inits such that they are as close as possible to the MLEs for that model. One common and important strategy is to use the estimates from a simpler model as the starting values for a more complex one. Hence, you could take the two intercepts from the first model as starting values for the intercepts in the second model and then augment these, at the correct positions in the list of inits, with sensible guesses of what the effect of veg_group2 might be (of course, on the logit link scale).

Sometimes problems are due to constellations with the particular data set. Can you report the sample sizes of your data set (number of sites and number of visits) and also report the estimates from model m1 ?

Best regards  --- Marc

I am using forward step wise regression by running models with each covariate, selecting the one with the lowest AIC, then running another set of models with the addition of each covariate, and continuing this process until I find the model with the covariates that produce the lowest AIC.
